candidates.name: Close-Grip Incline Bench Press

distinctFrom.why: incline bench angle shifts load toward the clavicular chest/front delts on top of the close grip's triceps bias; also distinct from Incline Barbell Bench Press by grip width

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Grip and bench angle both differ from any single existing row; rep/set defaults match the corpus's other close-grip pressing rows.

candidates.name: Wide-Grip Bench Press

distinctFrom.why: wider hand spacing shortens the range of motion and shifts emphasis toward the pecs, away from triceps; the mirror-image variant to Close-Grip Bench Press

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Common accessory/competition-grip variant; no new demand axis behaviour vs the flat bench press.

candidates.name: Paused Bench Press

distinctFrom.why: a dead-stop pause on the chest removes the stretch reflex, changing the strength demand at the bottom (EL-2 range/depth class)

sources: Mark Rippetoe, Starting Strength
NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Standard powerlifting-programme prescription; lower rep ceiling reflects the harder concentric off a static chest.

candidates.name: Pin Press (Bench)

distinctFrom.why: starts from a dead stop on safety pins at a settable height rather than a fixed board thickness resting on the chest; same triceps-lockout training purpose as Board Press, different apparatus and adjustability

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Position/floorAccess/axialLoad/balanceDemand came back null because the name lacks the literal phrase 'bench press'; overridden to match Barbell Bench Press's values since it is performed lying on a flat bench off safety pins.

candidates.name: Floor Press (Barbell)

distinctFrom.why: pressing from the floor removes leg drive and shortens the range where the upper arm meets the floor; mirrors the existing Floor Press (Dumbbell) but with a barbell

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Tagged chest-primary to match Floor Press (Dumbbell)'s convention, not triceps-primary like the close-grip floor press variant.

candidates.name: Spoto Press

distinctFrom.why: bar is paused an inch or two above the chest, never touching, removing the chest as a stopping/bouncing point (a distinct range/depth class from a paused-on-chest press)

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Named coaching-community pause variant, distinct from Paused Bench Press by depth (never touches). Demand axes overridden to match the flat bench press family (name has no 'bench press' phrase for the regex to key off).

candidates.name: Larsen Press

distinctFrom.why: legs are raised off the bench/floor, removing leg drive and arch entirely - a support/stability condition change, not merely cosmetic

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Demand axes overridden to match the flat bench press family; torso is still bench-supported even though the legs are not.

candidates.name: Close-Grip Decline Bench Press

distinctFrom.why: decline bench angle combined with the close grip; the decline changes the resistance curve at lockout the same way Decline Barbell Bench Press differs from the flat press

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Tagged triceps-primary/pushdown to match the Close-Grip Bench Press convention.

candidates.name: Seated Barbell Overhead Press

distinctFrom.why: seated removes leg drive and lower-back involvement in stabilising the bar, matching the existing standing/seated split used for Dumbbell Shoulder Press vs Seated Dumbbell Press

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: axialLoad came back null (the regex only flags 'standing' presses); overridden to true to match the existing curated values for Seated Dumbbell Press and Z-Press, which are seated overhead presses tagged axialLoad true.

candidates.name: Behind-the-Neck Press

distinctFrom.why: the bar travels behind the head rather than in front of the face, demanding a different shoulder external-rotation and thoracic-extension range

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: never_auto per EL-5's demanding-mobility caution. gripDemand derived as 'none' by a name-regex collision (the word 'neck' matches the neck-isolation grip-free rule) - flagged as a vocabulary/derivation gap; overridden to 'bar' since the lifter grips a loaded barbell throughout. axialLoad also came back null and is overridden to true (standing barbell load transmitted through the spine, same as any standing barbell press).

candidates.name: Pin Press (Overhead Press)

distinctFrom.why: starts from a dead stop on safety pins at a settable height, removing the stretch reflex and any leg-drive carryover into the pull off the shoulders

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: All demand axes resolved cleanly from the standing-press rules.

candidates.name: Low-Bar Back Squat

distinctFrom.why: bar sits lower on the rear delts, forcing a greater forward torso lean and hip-dominant moment; a materially different loading vector to the corpus's existing (higher-bar-style) generic Back Squat

sources: Mark Rippetoe, Starting Strength
NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: The existing 'Barbell Back Squat' is treated as the corpus's generic/high-bar-style entry; 'High-Bar Back Squat' and 'High Bar Squat' are recorded as aliases for it in aliasesForExisting rather than proposed as a second new row, since a plain high-bar squat is not mechanically distinguishable from the existing generic entry.

candidates.name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Barbell)

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (barbell on the back vs a dumbbell in each hand); bar path clearance behind the rear leg makes this a distinct, less common setup

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Rarer than the dumbbell version because of bar-path clearance, hence niche rather than specialist.

candidates.name: Barbell Walking Lunge

distinctFrom.why: continuous forward travel each rep rather than a stationary or reverse-stepping lunge, mirroring the corpus's own split of Dumbbell Lunge vs Walking Lunge

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Mirrors the dumbbell family's existing walking/reverse/static lunge split.

candidates.name: Barbell Reverse Lunge

distinctFrom.why: stepping backward changes the knee-shear and balance demand versus a forward or walking lunge, mirroring Dumbbell Reverse Lunge vs Dumbbell Lunge

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Mirrors the dumbbell family's existing walking/reverse/static lunge split.

candidates.name: Overhead Squat

distinctFrom.why: the bar is held overhead in a wide snatch grip rather than racked, adding a shoulder-stability and thoracic-mobility demand on top of the squat pattern

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Olympic-derived and technically demanding; never_auto per EL-5. All demand axes resolved cleanly.

candidates.name: Barbell Hack Squat

distinctFrom.why: free-weight implement (barbell held behind the calves) vs a fixed machine sled path; distinct balance and grip demand

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Historic barbell-behind-the-legs squat, largely superseded by the machine version but still occasionally programmed; gripDemand resolved to 'supportive' rather than 'bar' because the bar hangs behind straight arms rather than being gripped for a press or pull.

candidates.name: Snatch-Grip Romanian Deadlift

distinctFrom.why: a Romanian deadlift hip-hinge pattern (bar stays off the floor between reps, knees stay softer) performed with the wide snatch grip, versus the existing row's dead-stop-from-floor conventional-deadlift pattern

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Also distinct from Romanian Deadlift by grip width, which increases range of motion and upper-back demand.

candidates.name: Block Pull (Deadlift)

distinctFrom.why: the plates rest on blocks so the bar starts at a fixed height under real free-weight tension throughout, rather than resting on safety pins inside a power rack

sources: Bill Starr, The Strongest Shall Survive
NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Borderline distinction from Rack Pull - both are elevated-start pulls; flagged as a least-sure candidate in the final report.

candidates.name: Paused Deadlift

distinctFrom.why: a mid-pull pause (typically below the knee) removes momentum and adds a static-hold strength demand, a distinct range/depth class

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Common conjugate/powerlifting accessory prescription.

candidates.name: Barbell Glute Bridge

distinctFrom.why: performed with the upper back on the floor rather than on a bench, giving a shorter range of motion at the top and no bench-supported end-range overload; also distinct implement from the existing bodyweight Glute Bridge

sources: Bret Contreras, Glute Lab
candidates.notes: Beginner-friendly entry point before progressing to the bench-supported hip thrust.

candidates.name: Wide-Grip Barbell Curl

distinctFrom.why: a wider grip shifts emphasis toward the short head of the biceps to a greater degree than the standard grip

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Mirror-image variant to Close-Grip Barbell Curl.

candidates.name: Close-Grip Barbell Curl

distinctFrom.why: a closer-than-shoulder-width grip shifts emphasis toward the long head, the opposite bias to the wide-grip variant

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Tagged long_head subregion, mirroring Spider Curl's long-head bias.

candidates.name: Cheat Curl

distinctFrom.why: deliberate hip and torso momentum swings the bar past the sticking point, a ballistic character rather than a strict grind

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: never_auto per EL-5: ballistic character makes it unsuitable for unsupervised auto-programming.

candidates.name: Incline Skull Crusher (Barbell)

distinctFrom.why: incline bench angle changes the elbow moment through the range compared with the flat or decline versions already in the corpus

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: overheadPosition came back null; overridden to true to match Barbell Skull Crusher and Decline Skull Crusher, which are both tagged overheadPosition true for the same overhead-arm-extension phase.

candidates.name: Standing Barbell Overhead Tricep Extension

distinctFrom.why: performed standing with the bar lowered behind the head rather than lying down lowering to the forehead; a position change from lying to standing

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Fills the standing-barbell gap alongside the existing lying/decline skull crusher variants.

candidates.name: Donkey Calf Raise (Barbell)

distinctFrom.why: bent-over torso position loads the gastrocnemius through a longer stretch than an upright standing raise; implement also differs from the existing bodyweight and machine donkey calf raise rows

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Historically performed with a partner or hip belt for resistance; here loaded via a barbell on the back.

candidates.name: Barbell Rollout

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (loaded barbell vs a bodyweight ab wheel), changing the resistance profile and stability demand through the rollout

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: overheadPosition left null (not overridden): the existing corpus is itself inconsistent on this axis for rollout movements (Ab Rollout=true, Ab Wheel Rollout=false), so no confident value can be asserted here.

rejected.name: Bradford Press
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Bradford Press' — already exists in the corpus

rejected.name: Sissy Squat (Barbell)
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 — sissy squat is bodyweight-family per the brief, not a barbell-loaded movement in standard programming

rejected.name: Kroc Row (Barbell)
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 — Kroc-style high-rep rowing is a dumbbell-family movement per the brief

rejected.name: Tempo Squat (3-1-1)
rejected.reason: not representable — tempo is a set-level prescription, not a distinct exercise identity in this schema; Pause Squat already covers the one tempo variant the corpus programmes as a named lift

rejected.name: Reverse-Grip Incline Bench Press
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 — combines two existing variants (grip + angle) without evidence any programme writes this down as its own named lift
